title: Why Your New Classroom Management Plan Isn't Working
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin diagnoses why a newly taught classroom management plan can immediately fail despite careful preparation, teaching, and modeling. He identifies three possible causes: introducing the plan midyear after students have already learned the teacher doesn't follow through, a teacher's own lack of confidence that students sense even when unspoken, and a tentative delivery that unconsciously hedges and softens boundaries while gauging student reaction. Ultimately, he argues these specific reasons matter less than the underlying requirement: students must directly experience sustained consistency before they'll believe a teacher has genuinely changed, and no amount of preparation substitutes for that lived proof. The article encourages teachers to push through initial fumbling, doubt, and mistakes, insisting that consistent follow-through will eventually work even if the delivery itself is imperfect. It closes with an extended sailing metaphor about surviving early resistance to reach calmer waters, alongside an assertion that students secretly crave the discipline and belonging that come with high standards.
points: A new classroom management plan can fail immediately due to one of three causes: midyear introduction, a teacher's own lack of confidence, or a tentative, hedged delivery.
Students who have already learned that a teacher doesn't follow through will naturally test a newly introduced plan, since it contradicts prior experience.
Students can sense a lack of confidence through tone, posture, and nonverbal cues even when the teacher says nothing revealing outright.
None of the specific causes of early failure ultimately matter; what changes behavior is students directly experiencing sustained consistency over time.
Even an imperfect, nervous delivery of a new plan will eventually work if the teacher follows through consistently without retreating.
quotes: Not five minutes after teaching your plan, your students are right back at it; misbehaving as if nothing has changed. So what happened?
When through several months of the school year you show yourself to be one person, your students won’t believe you when you all of a sudden claim to be someone else.
However, your students can sense it. They feel it in their bones when you’re less than 100 percent committed. Show any weakness—tone of voice, posture, non-verbal expression—and they’ll know it.

You were lightening the shock of change . You were saying the right things but with caveats and qualifiers. You were warming them up to the idea of full accountability instead of sticking your flag in the ground.

You can be nervous and fumble over your words. You can be the worst communicator of all time and do all three of the above and then some. And although it may take longer, if you’re consistent, you’ll get there.

The truth is, they want discipline. They want high standards. They want to be part of something special. They crave it deep inside, beyond their awareness. It doesn’t matter who they are or where you work.
